body_html:
A mobile SEO checklist makes sure the mobile version of your site, which Google uses to crawl and index it, has the same content, links, and metadata as desktop, loads quickly on a phone, and is easy to use with a thumb. Here's what to check and how to fix common problems.

Why the mobile version is the one that counts

Google finished its move to mobile-first indexing in October 2023. In plain terms, Google crawls your site with a smartphone bot and builds its index from what that bot sees. If something exists on desktop but not on mobile, Google may not see it at all.

The testing tools changed too. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in Search Console in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. So mobile checks now run through Lighthouse, the URL Inspection tool, and a crawler set to a smartphone user agent.

The mobile SEO checklist

These items follow Google's mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices, plus the usability issues that come up most on real sites.

1. Same content on mobile and desktop

  • Main text and headings match. Tabs and accordions are fine, as long as the content is in the page.
  • Primary content doesn't load only after a tap, swipe, or click. Google's bot won't take those actions.
  • Images have the same alt text on both versions.
  • Mobile menus still link to your important pages. Trimmed-down mobile navigation is a common way category and service pages lose internal links.

2. Same metadata and structured data

  • Title tags and meta descriptions match desktop.
  • Robots meta tags match. A noindex or nofollow that only appears on mobile can drop pages from search.
  • Structured data appears on the mobile pages, not just desktop.

3. Resources Google can reach

Make sure robots.txt doesn't block the CSS, JavaScript, or image files your mobile pages need. Run a live test in URL Inspection and look at the screenshot: if the page looks broken or blank, Google is probably seeing it that way.

4. A layout built for phones

  • The page has a viewport meta tag set to the device width.
  • Nothing scrolls sideways.
  • Text is readable without pinching to zoom.
  • Buttons and links are big enough, and far enough apart, to tap accurately.

5. Speed on a phone

Core Web Vitals are Google's measures of loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP), and visual stability (CLS). web.dev sets the "good" marks at 2.5 seconds or less for LCP, 200 milliseconds or less for INP, and 0.1 or less for CLS. The Core Web Vitals report in Search Console shows mobile and desktop separately, and mobile is usually the weaker of the two. Oversized images, heavy sliders, and stacks of third-party scripts are the usual culprits. My page speed optimization work starts there.

6. No intrusive pop-ups

Google's guidance on intrusive interstitials and dialogs calls out full-screen pop-ups and dialogs that cover the content, such as newsletter or app-install prompts. Small banners that take up a fraction of the screen are fine. Interstitials a site is legally required to show, such as an age gate, are treated differently.

7. Separate mobile URLs, if you still have them

If your site uses a separate mobile domain (often m.yoursite.com), check that each desktop page links to its mobile twin with the right canonical and alternate tags, that robots.txt rules match, and that both versions are verified in Search Console. Google recommends responsive design, one URL that adapts to any screen, because it's the simplest to maintain.

How to find mobile SEO issues on your site

  1. URL Inspection live test. Shows the rendered page and HTML Google's smartphone bot sees.
  2. Lighthouse. Run it from Chrome DevTools in mobile mode, or through PageSpeed Insights, for speed and usability checks.
  3. Two crawls. Crawl once with a smartphone user agent and once with a desktop one, then compare word counts, titles, links, and structured data.
  4. Your own phone. Tap through your top pages and forms. Many problems are obvious in thirty seconds.

Is mobile-first indexing the same as being mobile-friendly?

No. Mobile-first indexing is about which version of your site Google reads: the mobile one. Mobile-friendliness is about whether people can comfortably use that version. A site can be indexed mobile-first and still frustrate visitors with tiny text or pop-ups. A good mobile SEO checklist covers both: content parity for indexing, and layout, speed, and usability for the people who land on the page.

Does Google still have a mobile-friendly test?

Not as a standalone tool. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in December 2023. For the same kinds of checks, use Lighthouse in Chrome or PageSpeed Insights for speed and usability, and the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to see the mobile page Google renders. Core Web Vitals data by device is still in Search Console.

Do you need responsive design for mobile SEO?

It isn't required, but Google recommends it. Responsive design uses one URL and one set of HTML for every screen size, so there's no risk of the mobile version falling out of sync with desktop. Separate mobile sites can still rank, but they need careful canonical tags, matching content, and matching robots rules, which adds ongoing work and more places for mistakes.
